thread.title: Fat Dividend Yields To Beef Up Your Portfolio In 2018

author: Colorado Wealth Management Fund
title: Fat Dividend Yields To Beef Up Your Portfolio In 2018
text:
This research report was produced by The REIT Forum with assistance from Big Dog Investments .
Many great dividend growth stocks focus on meeting simple needs of customers.
It should be no surprise that many dividend champions are consumer staples.
Without the great recession, some apartment REITs might be much further on the road to being dividend champions. The apartment REITs are a very attractive segment for investing.
Many income investors would consider a position in owning physical rental housing as a very reasonable part of their retirement plan. Purchasing a REIT that invests in that segment is a much simpler way to get the same exposure.
Investors can also find very solid dividend yields from preferred shares.
For investors interested in The REIT Forum’s preferred share ratings, see my guide to preferred shares . I also have a guide for preferred share dividend captures .
Apartment Investment & Management Company AIMCO ( AIV ) is a medium-sized apartment REIT with an investment grade balance sheet. They carry a risk rating of “2.5” which is the highest among the big 7 apartment REITs. For those that aren’t familiar with my rating system, here is a general guide:
Source: The REIT Forum
The apartment REIT sector is currently very attractive. A significant decline in the share prices of the apartment REITs created a great opportunity for long-term investors. The sector should witness solid average growth rates over the next few decades.
We can see AIV’s history of growth in AFFO per share and economic income:
Source: AIV investor presentation
The 5-year compound annual growth rate in AFFO was 10% while the economic return was 14%. The economic return is not a measure most equity REITs report. It uses management’s estimates of the net value of their assets and while adding in cash dividends.
AIV’s growth over the last 5 years has been quite favorable:
Source: AIV investor presentation
Using this arbitrary time period, AIV has performed exceptionally well compared to peers. If we modify the time period, the comparison would be more modest.
AIV carries a credit rating of BBB-:
Source: AIV investor presentation
The leverage for AIV is still reasonable, but it is a little higher than I would prefer. Their use of preferred equity is favorable for common shareholders because it reduces the risk of needing to refinance outstanding debts since the preferred shares do not have a maturity.
At a straight BBB rating, AIV would be materially more attractive as a long-term investment. The BBB rating (as opposed to BBB-) gives the REIT more flexibility if the economy worsens.
Full analysis on AIV (subscription to The REIT Forum required)
Philip Morris Philip Morris ( PM ) is a great dividend growth stock. They were spun off from Altria Group ( MO ). Neither company knows what it means to cut the dividend. Their dividends go in only one direction and that direction is up.
Philip Morris was relatively attractive before the Q1 2018 earnings release. When the company provided their Q1 release, it sent analysts into a panic. A reduction in the shipment volume of IQOS led to dramatically lower estimates for forward growth rates.
I don’t agree with the other analysts. They supported extremely high valuations for Philip Morris within the last 12 months. When their projections for the growth rate changed so dramatically, it suggests that the projections were terrible from the start.
Analysts were attempting to extrapolate too much information from the shipment volume for IQOS products. The result of their reliance on computer modeling for forward growth rates using shipment volumes leads to overconfidence.
When analysts have a complex model for forecasting growth rates, the appearance of precision can lead to a failure to dig deeper into the numbers.
A similar situation was observed in early 2017 with Target ( TGT ). Their CEO, Brian Cornell, got in front of the microphone and began educating analysts about all the problems Target faced. He provided dreadful earnings guidance that sent shares plummeting. Analysts simply updated their forward earnings estimates to be very similar to the guidance they were given. It appears very few of the Wall Street analysts actually attempted to run their own projections. They simply used management’s numbers and increased or decreased the estimate by a penny based on their outlook.
The impact of a small change to growth estimates is evidenced today in Tanger Factory Outlets ( SKT ). The shares plunged following a revision to guidance. The new guidance was lower by a little over 1%. Shares responded by falling around 10%.
There is no fundamental basis for that change in valuation. The decline in guidance was a negative, but it wasn’t worth a 10% decline in the share price.
It shouldn’t be a huge surprise that price targets swing wildly with growth rates. Lately, the most successful sectors have included the defense industry and technology. The tech stocks like Apple ( AAPL ), Google ( GOOG ), Facebook ( FB ), Microsoft ( MSFT ), Advanced Micro Devices ( AMD ), and Intel ( INTC ) trade strongly based off of future growth projections. The difficulty with placing too much emphasis on the projections is that they are rarely accurate. Growth may be above the projections or below the projections, but it will rarely match the projections perfectly. Often, company earnings are very similar to consensus forecasts. But the consensus forecast is generally built and modified in the year and months coming up to the announcement. Investors should not expect earnings for 2022 to be accurately forecasted today.
For example, AT&T ( T ) and Verizon ( VZ ) could see a material impact to their margins if Sprint ( S ) and T-Mobile ( TMUS ) are successful in their merger attempts. Some investors argue that a combined entity would be more effective at competing against Verizon and AT&T. They believe that an improvement in economies of scales would allow Sprint and T-Mobile to offer even lower prices as a combined entity.
I take the opposite view. I believe Verizon and AT&T would benefit significantly from the two smaller companies merging. A merger would lead to further concentration in a sector displaying oligopolistic tendencies.
Currently, the price-based competition is mostly between T-Mobile and Sprint. AT&T and Verizon have attempted to avoid this competition. A combined entity would have a larger incentive to raise prices and focus on expanding margins rather than growing market share.
MFA preferred share MFA Financial’s ( MFA ) preferred share is usually too expensive to start a position so I bought it even though it was within the hold range.
Source: CWMF’s subscriber spreadsheet (subscription required for 50+ preferred shares and baby bonds with comparing prices)
MFA does have a baby bond, MFO, but it’s currently in the sell range by $0.07.
MFA-B is sitting around the mid-range of a hold. MFA-B does carry a risk rating of “2”, so it’s a decent option for the conservative buy-and-hold investors. When the baby bond does come into the buy range, it’s nice to pick up a high yield with a risk rating of “1”.
There is no call protection on the calendar for either the baby bond or the preferred share:
Investors only have the 30-day notice a company will give on a call. However, we need to take a look at the accrued dividend. Since there is $0.39 of accumulation, the stripped price for MFA-B is around $24.74. Preferred shares trading at a discount to the call value of $25 is a form of call protection. Even if shares are called right away, there is a positive worst-cash-to-call of $0.25.
I may look to harvest gains if it gets a solid run higher perhaps around $25.35 to $25.45. I actively trade in preferred shares. For the B&H investor, it is nice to have a decent entry point. Normally, the higher price leads to too much call risk. Otherwise, it is a lower risk preferred share.
MFO is only a sell by $0.07, but it technically falls just within the range.
